Circuit history, confirmed players, tone recipes, 2019 reissue reviewed. admin 22 September 2026 26 min read Updated 26 September 2026 GG-ARTICLE-TOP Somewhere in the middle of 1976, in a studio in Brittania Row, London, David Gilmour plugged a battered violet-faced fuzz box into his Hiwatt and discovered the tone that would define an era. The pedal was a 1973 Electro-Harmonix Ram’s Head Big Muff Pi — already a few years old, already slightly unpredictable, already capable of sounds that no other piece of gear on the planet could produce. By the time Pink Floyd finished recording Animals and took the show on the road in 1977, that Ram’s Head was doing things to the fabric of rock guitar that nobody had quite heard before: soaring, sustained leads that seemed to bloom and breathe; a midrange character that cut through the biggest arena mix without a hint of harshness; a fuzz that felt somehow vocal, organic, alive. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO That specific pedal, and the circuit family it belongs to, has been haunting guitarists ever since. The Electro-Harmonix Ram’s Head Big Muff Pi is one of the most obsessively studied, most counterfeited, most lovingly reverse-engineered pedals in history — and for good reason. When Electro-Harmonix finally reissued it in 2019 in a compact nano chassis, Guitar World called it “arguably the most anticipated of the Big Muff reissues.” Half a century on from its original manufacture, the ram still rules. Jump to the Rig ↓ How to Get the Tone ↓ A Brief History of the Ram’s Head: The V2 Era (1973–1977) The Big Muff Pi was born in the late 1960s, designed by Electro-Harmonix founder Mike Matthews. The first production run, known among collectors as the Triangle — named by Big Muff historian Kit Rae for the triangular layout of the knobs — ran from approximately 1969 to 1973. It was warmer, more open, slightly less compressed than what came next. But it was the second generation, the Ram’s Head, that cemented the Big Muff’s place in guitar history.
